1345.title: Savitri at the banyan
1345.hook: a banyan wound with thread: how Savitri's story became a vrata, a vow kept with the body
1345.carry: a vrata turns a story into a vow
1345.howItsDone: On Vat Savitri, some married Hindu women fast, worship at a banyan tree, wind thread around its trunk and hear Savitri's story told, asking for long lives for their husbands; the day and customs differ by region.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-FORTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, satsang: on the road behind Death, Savitri showed that time near the good is never wasted.
screen: `TIME NEAR THE GOOD IS NEVER WASTED.`

segments.voice: A banyan tree, its trunk wound round and round with thread. On a festival day called Vat Savitri, some married Hindu women fast, walk around a banyan and tie thread to it, asking for long lives for their husbands. The tree doesn't come from the epic's telling; it comes from the way the story has been lived since. On our last day with her: how a story becomes a vow, and how one woman can be read more than one way.
screen: `A BANYAN WOUND WITH THREAD.` → `A FESTIVAL IN HER NAME.` → `ONE WOMAN, MORE THAN ONE READING.`

segments.voice: Start with where the epic puts her. The story sits in the Mahabharata's forest book, in a section whose title can be translated as the greatness of the devoted wife. The sage Markandeya tells it because Yudhishthira has asked: has there ever been a woman as devoted as Draupadi? His answer is Savitri, and his last word is that Draupadi, like Savitri, will save them all. So the frame is devotion, and some readers keep it: a wife whose faithfulness is strong enough to stop Death. Others hear a woman of fierce will and a sharp mind, who chose her own husband, kept a hard truth alone for a year, and argued with Death on the road. A modern poet, Aurobindo, read her as the divine word come down to free the soul from death. Now the teaching. Hinduism has a name for what happens at the banyan: a vrata, a vow. You choose a day, you fast or keep a rule, you do a puja, and you hear the story the vow belongs to, its vrat katha, told out loud. Hindus keep vratas for Shiva, for the Goddess, on Ekadashi, for the people they love. On Vat Savitri, the story is Savitri's. And Savitri kept one herself: before the day Death came, the epic says, she held a three-night vow, fasting and standing still like a post. The women at the tree are doing a smaller version of what she did. That's the gift of a vrata in a busy life. Love that would stay a feeling becomes a day you keep, with an empty stomach and a thread in your hand.
screen: `THE GREATNESS OF THE DEVOTED WIFE` · `DEVOTION, WILL, THE DIVINE WORD` · `VRATA: A FAST, A PUJA, A STORY TOLD` · `SAVITRI KEPT ONE HERSELF` · then, large: `A VRATA TURNS A STORY INTO A VOW.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose life you'd ask to be long, and hold their face for a moment. Then, slowly, as if winding thread around a banyan, go round them in your mind, their morning, their work, their evening, their sleep, one slow circle for each breath. If you pray, you can pray for them, the way the women at the tree do.
Savitri. Told as the greatness of a devoted wife, read by others as a woman of will, and kept each year in a vrata at a banyan wound with thread.
screen: `SAVITRI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a vrata turns a story into a vow. Savitri's became a thread around a banyan. Rest well.

1346.title: Damayanti's act of truth
1346.hook: five men with one face, and Damayanti finds the real one by the power of truth
1346.carry: satya, truth, has a power of its own
1346.howItsDone: Hindus hear Damayanti's story in the Mahabharata's forest book, where the sage Brihadashva tells it to Yudhishthira; it is also retold in later poems, plays and dance across India.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-FORTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a vrata turns a story into a vow: at the banyan, Savitri's story is still kept as a vrata. Today, a new woman, and a hall full of gods.
screen: `A VRATA TURNS A STORY INTO A VOW.`

segments.voice: Five men in a row, every one with the same face. That's what Damayanti sees when she walks into her own swayamvara, garland in hand, ready to choose. Four of them are gods wearing the face of the man she loves. One of them is the man. Last year we heard the whole story of Nala and Damayanti, from a golden swan to a long reunion. This time we stay with her: three days, three choices, and the first is made in a hall full of gods.
screen: `FIVE MEN, ONE FACE.` → `FOUR GODS AND A MAN.` → `HER FIRST CHOICE.`

segments.voice: Damayanti is the daughter of King Bhima of Vidarbha. She has chosen Nala in her heart before she ever sees him, because a swan carried his praises to her. Then four gods want her too: Indra, Agni, Varuna and Yama. They even make Nala carry their offer, and she tells him plainly: she is his. On the day, the gods come wearing Nala's face. She can't tell them apart, so she doesn't guess. She bows to the gods in her heart and speaks a chain of truths. In paraphrase: as I have never strayed from Nala in word or thought, by that truth, let the gods show him to me. As I took this vow to honor him, by that truth, let them show themselves. And they do. The gods don't sweat. Their eyes don't blink. Their garlands stay fresh, no dust touches them, and they cast no shadow. One figure has a shadow, dust and a wilting garland. That's the one she garlands, and the gods bless the couple. Here's the teaching. In Hinduism, satya, truth, isn't only good manners. It has a power of its own. A truth lived all the way through can move even the gods, and Hindu stories come back to this again and again. The Mundaka Upanishad says it in three words, satyam eva jayate: truth alone wins. Those words sit under India's national emblem today. And Gandhi named his whole nonviolent struggle satyagraha, holding fast to truth. Damayanti had no army in that hall. She had a promise she had never broken, and she said it out loud.
screen: `BY THAT TRUTH, SHOW YOURSELVES` · `NO SWEAT, NO BLINK, NO SHADOW` · `SATYAM EVA JAYATE: TRUTH ALONE WINS` · then, large: `SATYA, TRUTH, HAS A POWER OF ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus begin a puja with a sankalpa, a short spoken intention. Make one now: one true thing you mean to keep today, small enough to really keep. Say it once, quietly, then let your breath settle around it for a few breaths. If you pray, you can offer it to God; if you don't, just hold it.
Damayanti. The princess of Vidarbha who spoke her truth to the gods, and found the man with a shadow.
screen: `DAMAYANTI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: satya, truth, has a power of its own. Damayanti's moved the gods. See you tomorrow.

1347.title: Kali leaves Nala
1347.hook: Damayanti sends out a question, and on the road to her, Kali finally lets Nala go
1347.carry: hearing a sacred story is a shelter
1347.howItsDone: Hindus know Damayanti's search from the Mahabharata's forest book, where Brihadashva tells it to the exiled Yudhishthira; it is also retold in later poems, plays and dance.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-FORTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, satya, truth, has a power of its own: by Damayanti's act of truth, the gods showed themselves.
screen: `SATYA, TRUTH, HAS A POWER OF ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: How do you find someone who doesn't want to be found? Damayanti's husband lost everything at dice, walked into the forest with her, cut their one shared cloth while she slept, and left. She survived the forest and made her way home to her father's house in Vidarbha, to her children. Nala is out there somewhere, changed, hidden, ashamed. A king's daughter could send riders. Damayanti sends something smaller and sharper. And on the road back to her, something finally lets him go.
screen: `HE DOESN'T WANT TO BE FOUND.` → `HOME IN VIDARBHA.` → `SHE SENDS SOMETHING SHARPER.`

segments.voice: She calls Brahmanas, travelers who go from court to court, and gives them a question to repeat wherever people gather. In paraphrase: where have you gone, gambler, after cutting half the cloth of the wife who loved you and leaving her asleep in the forest? Have mercy, and answer. In a far city, a plain charioteer answers it, and Damayanti knows. So she sets a trap made of love: word goes out that she'll choose a husband again tomorrow, so soon that only Nala's driving could bring a king there in time. On that wild drive, King Rituparna teaches his charioteer the secret of dice, and the moment Nala knows it, Kali comes out of him. Not the goddess Kali; a different name. This Kali is the spirit of strife, and the same word names the dark age, Kali Yuga. He had slipped into Nala through one small lapse, and it was with Kali inside him that Nala gambled away his kingdom and left his wife. Leaving, Kali makes Nala a promise: people who tell your story with care won't need to fear me. The whole tale is being told to Yudhishthira in exile, a king who has also just lost everything at dice, to comfort him. Here's the teaching. Many Hindu texts close with a phala-shruti, the fruit of hearing: a blessing promised to whoever listens. Nala's story carries one in Kali's own mouth. A sacred story isn't only a record; hearing it is a kind of shelter. Some Hindu families still read Nala's story in a bad stretch of life, and in parts of South India it's tied to hard times under the planet Shani. Back in Vidarbha, Damayanti sends their children to the charioteer, and watches him weep.
screen: `ONE QUESTION, CARRIED FAR` · `ON THE ROAD, KALI LEAVES HIM` · `TELL HIS STORY, AND DON'T FEAR ME` · then, large: `HEARING A SACRED STORY IS A SHELTER.`

segments.voice: If you're in a hard stretch, name it to yourself in one plain line. Then, the way families read Nala's story in bad times, tell yourself the shape of his: everything lost, hidden, ashamed, and still searched for and found. Hold that shape beside yours for a few breaths. If you pray, you can ask for strife to leave your house.

1348.title: Witnessed by the gods
1348.hook: face to face at last, Nala questions Damayanti's faith, and a god answers for her
1348.carry: a marriage is vowed with the gods as witness
1348.howItsDone: Hindus know Nala and Damayanti's reunion from the Mahabharata's forest book; the sage tells it to Yudhishthira, who had also lost his kingdom at dice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hearing a sacred story is a shelter: on Damayanti's search, Kali left Nala with a promise for anyone who tells his story.
screen: `HEARING A SACRED STORY IS A SHELTER.`

segments.voice: Nala and Damayanti are face to face at last, in her father's house, after the forest, the cut cloth, the long separation. He still wears the changed, unlovely shape that has hidden him. And the hardest thing he says is a question for her: how could a faithful wife send out word that she'd choose another husband? The man who walked away is asking her to account for herself. Her third choice: what to say to that.
screen: `FACE TO FACE AT LAST.` → `HE ASKS THE HARD QUESTION.` → `HER THIRD CHOICE.`

segments.voice: When she sees him, she speaks with grief and no softening: what kind of man leaves a sleeping wife alone in the forest? Nala tells her it wasn't fully him: Kali had been inside him, and now Kali is gone. Then he asks his question. How could a faithful wife announce she'd choose again? Damayanti answers it straight. It was never real. It was a way to bring him to Vidarbha, because only he could drive a king there in a single day. And then she does what Hindu stories do with the deepest promises: she calls the gods to witness. In paraphrase: let the Wind, who moves through this whole world, take my life if I have done wrong. The Wind answers, a voice from the sky: she has kept faith with you the whole time. Only then does Nala put on the serpent's garment and become himself again. Here's the teaching. A Hindu marriage isn't only an agreement between two people. It's a vow made in front of the gods. That's why, at a Hindu wedding, the couple walk around a sacred fire. Agni, the fire god, is the witness; Hindus say the vows are made agni sakshi, with the fire as witness. Agni was in the hall the day Damayanti chose Nala, and blessed them. Years later, the Wind spoke up for her. Many teachers read it this way: the gods who witness a vow also keep watch over it. So when you see a couple circling the fire, it isn't for the photos. Two people are asking a god to watch them keep their word.

segments.voice: A newborn lies alone on a riverbank in the forest. No mother nearby. No village. And around her, keeping off whatever might come out of the trees, are birds. That's how the Mahabharata's first book begins the life of Shakuntala, a stranger start than the love story people remember. A king will come. Today we stay before he arrives, with a girl, the birds, and the old hermit who heard her cry.
screen: `A NEWBORN ON A RIVERBANK.` → `BIRDS STANDING GUARD.` → `BEFORE THE KING ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: In the epic, Shakuntala tells her own beginning to a visitor, the way she heard it from the sage Kanva, who raised her. It starts with another sage, Vishvamitra, whose austerities are so fierce that Indra, king of the gods, grows afraid of his power. Indra sends the apsara Menaka, a celestial dancer, to break his concentration. She does. A daughter is born. Menaka leaves the baby beside a river in the forest and goes back to heaven. So the girl's parents are a great sage and a heavenly woman, and neither stays. Then the birds gather around the baby and protect her in that lonely place. Kanva, out for his bath, finds her, brings her home to his hermitage and raises her as his daughter. He names her for the birds: the epic's word for bird is shakunta, so she is Shakuntala, the one the birds protected. Then Kanva says the line this day is built on. The dharma texts, he says, count three as a father: the one who gives the body, the one who saves a life, and the one who gives food. By that measure, he is fully her father. That's the teaching, in the tradition's own words: in dharma, a parent is made by giving life, by keeping safe and by feeding, not by birth alone. And it lands right in modern families. An uncle who raised a nephew, a stepdad who packed the lunches, a grandmother who fed a child through the hard years: Kanva's words already count them. Her name doesn't remember her famous parents. It remembers the birds who stood guard, and the old man who chose her.

segments.voice: Who is here? That's the first thing King Dushyanta says at the hermitage. He has been hunting, has left his soldiers behind, and walks into the quiet place where the sage Kanva lives and calls out. Kanva isn't home. A young woman comes out instead, dressed like an ascetic, and welcomes him the way a host should. Then the king proposes marriage, almost at once, and the story waits to see what she'll say. What she says is not quite yes.
screen: `WHO IS HERE?` → `THE SAGE IS AWAY.` → `NOT QUITE YES.`

segments.voice: First, the welcome. Shakuntala offers the king a seat and water and asks after his health, the duties of a host, and tells him her father has gone to gather fruit. The king asks who she is, and she tells him her birth: the sage, the apsara, the birds. Then he asks her to marry him. Her first answer is patience. Wait for my father, she says. He will give me to you. The king answers with dharma. The old law books, he says, count eight forms of marriage. In some, a father gives his daughter away with rites and gifts. One, the gandharva, is made by two people's own choice, and it's lawful for a king. She can give herself. Here's the teaching under the scene: Hindu tradition has long made room for a marriage of the couple's own choosing, right there in its law books, beside the marriages families arrange. And Shakuntala does the thing the rest of her story hangs on. She agrees, on one condition: promise that the son born of me will be your heir. The king promises. They marry. He leaves for his city, saying he'll send an escort. Then Kanva comes home. The epic says he knows what happened through his own inner sight, and he isn't angry; he blesses her and calls the marriage a good one. Today, in plenty of Indian families, love marriage and arranged marriage still get argued over at dinner. It's an old conversation, and the epic has a word in it: a love match has its place, and Shakuntala made hers with a promise out loud. And from the city, nobody comes.

segments.voice: A crowded royal hall, and a woman holding a boy by the hand. No one ever came from the city, so Kanva has sent Shakuntala and her son to the king. She bows and says it plainly: this is your son. Make him your heir, as you promised me at the hermitage. King Dushyanta looks at her and says he doesn't know her, never married her, has no idea who she is. Everyone is watching. What does she do now?
screen: `I DON'T REMEMBER YOU.` → `THIS IS YOUR SON.` → `EVERYONE IS WATCHING.`

segments.voice: For a moment, the epic says, she can't move. She stands there stunned, ashamed and furious at once. Then she speaks, for a long time. Here is some of it, in paraphrase. First, witnesses. You think you're alone with what you did, she tells him, but the sun and the moon, the wind and fire, the earth and the sky, your own heart, all of them saw. Then the boy. She reminds the king of an old Vedic verse: from my limbs you are born, from my heart you arise; you are my own self, called son. When the king answers with insults about her mother and her birth in the forest, she turns his words around: you see others' faults as small as a mustard seed, and miss your own, as big as a bilva fruit. She never begs. Then a voice from the sky tells the king she speaks the truth, and the boy is his. Only then does Dushyanta take them in. Here's the teaching. That verse is older than the story. In the Vedic household rites, a father says it over his newborn, and again when he comes home from a journey and breathes in the scent of his child's head. In Hindu thought, a child isn't a possession or a stranger. A child is your own self, born again, and no father can say he doesn't know his own self. Plenty of Hindu parents and grandparents still greet a child by breathing in the top of their head, whether or not they know the verse. The old rite ends with a blessing: live a hundred autumns.
